items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An electron-rich species with a lone pair that it donates to an electron-deficient atom to form a new covalent bond"?
items.answer: nucleophile
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of nucleophile.

items.stem: Explain why polar bonds tend to break heterolytically.
items.answer: The more electronegative atom already has a greater share of the bonding pair, so it tends to take both electrons when the bond breaks, forming ions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The more electronegative atom already has a greater share of the bonding pair, so it tends to take both electrons when the bond breaks, forming ions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "All negative ions are electrophiles." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Negative ions with lone pairs are nucleophiles; electrophiles are electron-deficient (often positive).
items.markingKey: Negative ions with lone pairs are nucleophiles; electrophiles are electron-deficient (often positive). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe, in words, the curly arrows needed to show the first step of the reaction between CN⁻ and 2-chlorobutane (CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃).
items.answer: An arrow from a lone pair on CN⁻ to the δ+ carbon bonded to Cl; an arrow from the C–Cl bond to the Cl atom.
items.markingKey: Arrow from lone pair (not charge) of CN⁻ to C (1); arrow from C–Cl bond to Cl (1).

items.stem: What are the products of heterolytic fission of the C–Cl in chloromethane bond?
items.answer: CH₃⁺ and Cl⁻
items.markingKey: D. The more electronegative atom takes both bonding electrons.

items.stem:
The initial rate of hydrolysis of 1-bromobutane (RBr) by hydroxide ions was measured at 298 K.

experiment | [RBr] / mol dm⁻³ | [OH⁻] / mol dm⁻³ | initial rate / mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
1 | 0.0100 | 0.0100 | 1.73 × 10⁻⁷
2 | 0.0200 | 0.0100 | 3.45 × 10⁻⁷
3 | 0.0100 | 0.0200 | 3.45 × 10⁻⁷

(a) Deduce the orders with respect to RBr and OH⁻. [2]
(b) Write the rate equation and calculate k with units. [3]
(c) Deduce the mechanism and explain how the data support it. [2]
(d) Explain why the temperature of the reaction mixtures was controlled. [1]
items.answer: (a) 1 and 1 (b) rate = k[RBr][OH⁻]; k = 0.00173 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (c) SN2: both RBr and OH⁻ in one concerted step (d) The rate constant depends strongly on temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] exp 1→2: rate ×2 → first order in RBr (A1); exp 1→3: rate ×2 → order 1 in OH⁻ (A1). (b) [3] rate equation (A1); k = 0.00173 (A1) dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (A1). (c) [2] SN2 (1); link to orders (1). (d) [1] k varies with T (1).

items.stem: Define the term "heterolytic fission".
items.answer: The breaking of a covalent bond in which both electrons go to one atom, forming a cation and an anion
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the breaking of a covalent bond in which both electrons go to one atom, forming a cation and an anion. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: In heterolytic fission of C–Br, which atom takes the bonding pair?
items.answer: bromine
items.markingKey: C. More electronegative atom.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an electrophile and a nucleophile.
items.answer: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor attracted to δ+ centres; an electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions.
items.markingKey: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor attracted to δ+ centres; an electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why are carbocations electrophiles?
options: The positive carbon has an incomplete octet and accepts an electron pair.
items.answer: The positive carbon has an incomplete octet and accepts an electron pair.
items.markingKey: A. Six electrons.

items.stem: A student claims: "Curly arrows show the movement of atoms." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Curly arrows show the movement of electron pairs, not atoms.
items.markingKey: Curly arrows show the movement of electron pairs, not atoms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why water can act as a nucleophile.
items.answer: The oxygen atom has two lone pairs and a partial negative charge, so it can donate a lone pair to an electron-deficient carbon.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The oxygen atom has two lone pairs and a partial negative charge, so it can donate a lone pair to an electron-deficient carbon. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of CH₃⁺, H⁺, H⁻ (from NaBH₄) and the δ+ carbon of C–Br can act as a nucleophile?
items.answer: H⁻ (from NaBH₄)
items.markingKey: B. H⁻ (from NaBH₄) has a lone pair to donate.

items.stem: Classify each species as a nucleophile or electrophile: NH₃, H⁺, Br⁻, CH₃⁺, H₂O, NO₂⁺.
items.answer: nucleophiles: NH₃, Br⁻, H₂O; electrophiles: H⁺, CH₃⁺, NO₂⁺
items.markingKey: nucleophiles: NH₃, Br⁻, H₂O; electrophiles: H⁺, CH₃⁺, NO₂⁺

items.stem: Draw curly arrows to show the heterolytic fission of the C–Br bond in 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
items.answer: Arrow from C–Br bond to Br; (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻
items.markingKey: Arrow from C–Br bond to Br; (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻

items.stem: Describe, in words, the curly arrows needed to show the first step of the reaction between NH₃ and chloromethane (CH₃Cl).
items.answer: An arrow from a lone pair on NH₃ to the δ+ carbon bonded to Cl; an arrow from the C–Cl bond to the Cl atom.
items.markingKey: Arrow from lone pair (not charge) of NH₃ to C (1); arrow from C–Cl bond to Cl (1).

items.stem: Bromoethane reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions. (a) Identify the nucleophile and the electrophilic centre. (b) Explain why the carbon is electrophilic. (c) Draw the mechanism with curly arrows. (d) Name the organic product and state the type of reaction.
items.answer: (a) OH⁻; the carbon bonded to Br. (b) Br is more electronegative → C δ+. (c) arrow from OH⁻ lone pair to C; arrow from C–Br bond to Br; transition state; products. (d) ethanol; nucleophilic substitution.
items.markingKey: (a) OH⁻; the carbon bonded to Br. (b) Br is more electronegative → C δ+. (c) arrow from OH⁻ lone pair to C; arrow from C–Br bond to Br; transition state; products. (d) ethanol; nucleophilic substitution.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The nucleophile/electrophile classification is more useful than the Lewis acid/base classification in organic chemistry."
items.answer: They describe the same electron-pair donation; nucleophile/electrophile is simply the organic chemist’s language for it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: focuses on attack on carbon, explaining mechanisms; directly linked to curly-arrow mechanisms. Arguments against: it is essentially the same idea as Lewis theory; Lewis theory is more general across inorganic chemistry. Supported judgement: They describe the same electron-pair donation; nucleophile/electrophile is simply the organic chemist’s language for it. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The highest-energy, partially bonded arrangement of atoms in a reaction step"?
items.answer: transition state
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of transition state.

items.stem: Briefly explain why primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2 rather than SN1.
items.answer: Primary carbocations are very unstable (only one electron-releasing alkyl group), and the carbon is not crowded, so the nucleophile can attack from the back in a single step.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Primary carbocations are very unstable (only one electron-releasing alkyl group), and the carbon is not crowded, so the nucleophile can attack from the back in a single step. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "In SN1 the nucleophile and the halogenoalkane collide in the rate-determining step." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: In SN1 the slow step involves only the halogenoalkane ionising; the nucleophile reacts in the fast second step.
items.markingKey: In SN1 the slow step involves only the halogenoalkane ionising; the nucleophile reacts in the fast second step. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State the mechanism and rate equation for the hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane by aqueous NaOH.
items.answer: SN1; rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]
items.markingKey: SN1; rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]

items.stem: What is the organic product when chloromethane reacts with warm aqueous sodium hydroxide?
items.answer: methanol
items.markingKey: B. The nucleophile replaces the halogen: methanol.

items.stem: By which mechanism does 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, mainly react with aqueous hydroxide ions?
items.answer: SN1
items.markingKey: A. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary → SN1.

items.stem: (R)-2-bromobutane is hydrolysed under two different conditions. (a) Draw the SN2 mechanism and state the stereochemistry of the product. (b) Draw the SN1 mechanism and explain the stereochemistry of the product. (c) Write rate equations for both. (d) Suggest how the conditions could favour SN1.
items.answer: (a) backside attack, inversion → (S)-butan-2-ol. (b) planar secondary carbocation, attack from both faces → racemic butan-2-ol. (c) SN2 rate = k[RBr][OH⁻]; SN1 rate = k[RBr]. (d) polar protic solvent (water), weak nucleophile, low [OH⁻].
items.markingKey: (a) backside attack, inversion → (S)-butan-2-ol. (b) planar secondary carbocation, attack from both faces → racemic butan-2-ol. (c) SN2 rate = k[RBr][OH⁻]; SN1 rate = k[RBr]. (d) polar protic solvent (water), weak nucleophile, low [OH⁻].

items.answer: (a) 1 and 0 (b) rate = k[RBr]; k = 1.94 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (c) SN1: only RBr in the rate-determining step (carbocation formation) (d) The rate constant depends strongly on temperature.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "transition state".
items.answer: The highest-energy, partially bonded arrangement of atoms in a reaction step
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the highest-energy, partially bonded arrangement of atoms in a reaction step. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "inversion of configuration"?
options: An electron-rich species with a lone pair that it donates to an electron-deficient atom to form a new covalent bond
A two-step unimolecular nucleophilic substitution in which the leaving group departs first to form a carbocation, which is then attacked by the nucleophile
The reversal of the 3D arrangement around a chiral carbon (like an umbrella turning inside out) that occurs in SN2
The relative ability of a species to donate a lone pair to carbon in a substitution reaction
items.answer: The reversal of the 3D arrangement around a chiral carbon (like an umbrella turning inside out) that occurs in SN2
items.markingKey: C. "inversion of configuration" is the reversal of the 3D arrangement around a chiral carbon (like an umbrella turning inside out) that occurs in SN2.

items.stem: Why does steric hindrance slow SN2 reactions?
options: It makes the C–X bond stronger.
Bulky groups block the nucleophile’s approach to the back of the carbon.
items.answer: Bulky groups block the nucleophile’s approach to the back of the carbon.
items.markingKey: D. Backside attack blocked.

items.stem: Distinguish between a transition state and a carbocation intermediate.
items.answer: A transition state is an energy maximum with partial bonds; a carbocation is an intermediate in an energy minimum between two transition states.
items.markingKey: A transition state is an energy maximum with partial bonds; a carbocation is an intermediate in an energy minimum between two transition states. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In an SN2 transition state, how many groups are partially or fully bonded to the central carbon?
items.answer: five
items.markingKey: A. Nu···C···X plus three substituents.

items.stem: Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes do not react by SN2.
items.answer: Three bulky alkyl groups block the backside approach of the nucleophile to the carbon (steric hindrance).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Three bulky alkyl groups block the backside approach of the nucleophile to the carbon (steric hindrance). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Noah writes: "In SN1 the nucleophile and the halogenoalkane collide in the rate-determining step." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: In SN1 the slow step involves only the halogenoalkane ionising; the nucleophile reacts in the fast second step.
items.markingKey: In SN1 the slow step involves only the halogenoalkane ionising; the nucleophile reacts in the fast second step. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: (S)-2-iodobutane reacts with hydroxide ions by an SN1 mechanism. Predict the stereochemistry of the product and explain your answer.
items.answer: racemic butan-2-ol (equal amounts of (R) and (S)): the planar carbocation intermediate is attacked equally from both faces.
items.markingKey: racemic butan-2-ol (equal amounts of (R) and (S)) (1); the planar carbocation intermediate is attacked equally from both faces (1–2).

items.stem: What is the rate equation for the reaction of 1-bromopropane with excess ammonia in ethanol?
items.answer: rate = k[C₃H₇Br][NH₃]
items.markingKey: D. Primary → SN2: both reactants in the one step.

items.stem: By which mechanism does 1-chlorobutane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl, mainly react with aqueous hydroxide ions?
items.answer: SN2
items.markingKey: D. 1-chlorobutane is primary → SN2.

items.stem: Draw the SN2 mechanism for bromoethane with OH⁻, including the transition state.
items.answer: Arrow from OH⁻ to C; arrow C–Br → Br; transition state [HO···CH₂(CH₃)···Br]⁻ with partial bonds; products ethanol + Br⁻
items.markingKey: Arrow from OH⁻ to C; arrow C–Br → Br; transition state [HO···CH₂(CH₃)···Br]⁻ with partial bonds; products ethanol + Br⁻

items.stem: (R)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane reacts with hydroxide ions by an SN1 mechanism. Predict the stereochemistry of the product and explain your answer.
items.answer: racemic 3-methylhexan-3-ol (equal amounts of (R) and (S)): the planar carbocation intermediate is attacked equally from both faces.
items.markingKey: racemic 3-methylhexan-3-ol (equal amounts of (R) and (S)) (1); the planar carbocation intermediate is attacked equally from both faces (1–2).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The SN1/SN2 classification fully explains nucleophilic substitution."
items.answer: The two limiting mechanisms are very useful but real reactions often lie between them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains the effect of substrate structure, kinetics and stereochemistry; predicts rate equations. Arguments against: many secondary substrates react by mixed mechanisms; solvent effects and ion pairs complicate the picture; elimination competes. Supported judgement: The two limiting mechanisms are very useful but real reactions often lie between them.

items.answer: Stereochemical inversion is compelling, but together with kinetic data it provides the strongest case.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The ease with which a group departs with the bonding pair; better leaving groups form weaker bonds to carbon and stable anions (I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻)"?
items.answer: leaving group ability
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of leaving group ability.

items.stem: "Chloroalkanes are hydrolysed fastest because the C–Cl bond is the most polar of the C–Cl, C–Br and C–I bonds." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Rate depends mainly on bond strength; C–I is weakest, so iodoalkanes react fastest.
items.markingKey: Rate depends mainly on bond strength; C–I is weakest, so iodoalkanes react fastest. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why hydroxide ions are better nucleophiles than water molecules.
items.answer: OH⁻ carries a full negative charge, so its lone pairs are more available and it is more strongly attracted to the δ+ carbon. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Which of 1-bromobutane, 1-fluorobutane and 1-chlorobutane is hydrolysed fastest by aqueous hydroxide ions under the same conditions?
options: they all react at the same rate
items.answer: 1-bromobutane
items.markingKey: A. Bond enthalpies / kJ mol⁻¹: C–Br 285, C–F 492, C–Cl 324. Weaker bond → faster substitution.

items.stem: For the substitution reaction of 2-bromopropane (secondary) with hydroxide ions, what is the effect of raising the temperature by 10 °C?
options: has little effect on the rate
has no effect on the rate
items.answer: increases the rate
items.markingKey: D. raising the temperature by 10 °C: SN1 rate depends only on [RX] and carbocation formation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Bond enthalpy is the single most important factor in the rate of nucleophilic substitution."
items.answer: Bond enthalpy dominates the halogen trend, but structure, nucleophile and solvent are equally important overall.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains I > Br > Cl > F trend clearly; affects both SN1 and SN2. Arguments against: substrate structure (1°/2°/3°) changes the mechanism and rate hugely; nucleophile and solvent effects can be large; polarity plays some role. Supported judgement: Bond enthalpy dominates the halogen trend, but structure, nucleophile and solvent are equally important overall.

items.stem: Which halogenoalkane is hydrolysed fastest by aqueous OH⁻?
items.answer: 1-iodobutane
items.markingKey: C. C–I weakest bond.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "nucleophilicity".
items.answer: The relative ability of a species to donate a lone pair to carbon in a substitution reaction

items.stem: Explain the difference between a protic solvent and an aprotic solvent.
items.answer: A protic solvent has O–H or N–H bonds and solvates anions strongly (favours SN1); an aprotic solvent lacks them and leaves nucleophiles more reactive (favours SN2).
items.markingKey: A protic solvent has O–H or N–H bonds and solvates anions strongly (favours SN1); an aprotic solvent lacks them and leaves nucleophiles more reactive (favours SN2). items.stem: Why is fluoroethane almost inert to hydrolysis?

The C–F bond is very strong.

items.stem: Briefly explain why aprotic solvents favour SN2 reactions.
items.answer: They do not hydrogen-bond to the nucleophile, so the anion is less solvated and more reactive towards the carbon.

items.stem: "Bond enthalpy is the single most important factor in the rate of nucleophilic substitution." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Bond enthalpy dominates the halogen trend, but structure, nucleophile and solvent are equally important overall.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains I > Br > Cl > F trend clearly; affects both SN1 and SN2. items.stem: Which mechanism is typical for a tertiary halogenoalkane?
items.answer: SN1
items.markingKey: B. Stable 3° carbocation, steric hindrance.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "nucleophile"?
options: The highest-energy, partially bonded arrangement of atoms in a reaction step
The atom or group (e.g. a halide ion) that departs with the bonding pair when a bond breaks heterolytically
A polar solvent without O–H or N–H bonds (e.g. propanone) that does not solvate nucleophiles strongly; favours SN2
An electron-rich species with a lone pair that it donates to an electron-deficient atom to form a new covalent bond
items.answer: An electron-rich species with a lone pair that it donates to an electron-deficient atom to form a new covalent bond
items.markingKey: D. "nucleophile" is an electron-rich species with a lone pair that it donates to an electron-deficient atom to form a new covalent bond.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "protic solvent"?
options: A two-step unimolecular nucleophilic substitution in which the leaving group departs first to form a carbocation, which is then attacked by the nucleophile
An ion with a positively charged carbon atom that has only three bonds (six outer electrons)
A solvent with O–H or N–H bonds (e.g. water, ethanol) that can hydrogen-bond to ions; favours SN1
A polar solvent without O–H or N–H bonds (e.g. propanone) that does not solvate nucleophiles strongly; favours SN2
items.answer: A solvent with O–H or N–H bonds (e.g. water, ethanol) that can hydrogen-bond to ions; favours SN1
items.markingKey: C. "protic solvent" is a solvent with O–H or N–H bonds (e.g. water, ethanol) that can hydrogen-bond to ions; favours SN1.

items.stem: Distinguish between a carbocation intermediate and a transition state.
items.answer: A transition state is an energy maximum with partial bonds; a carbocation is an intermediate in an energy minimum between two transition states.
items.markingKey: A transition state is an energy maximum with partial bonds; a carbocation is an intermediate in an energy minimum between two transition states. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is NH₃ a nucleophile but NH₄⁺ is not?
options: NH₃ has a lone pair; in NH₄⁺ all electron pairs are bonding.
items.answer: NH₃ has a lone pair; in NH₄⁺ all electron pairs are bonding.
items.markingKey: A. Lone pair needed.

items.stem: Why does the rate of SN1 depend on the stability of the carbocation?
options: The leaving group is a carbocation.
Carbocation formation is the rate-determining step; a more stable carbocation forms faster.
items.answer: Carbocation formation is the rate-determining step; a more stable carbocation forms faster.
items.markingKey: D. Rate-determining step.

items.stem: Distinguish between SN1 and SN2.
items.answer: SN1: two steps via a carbocation, rate = k[RX], favoured by tertiary substrates, racemisation; SN2: one concerted step, rate = k[RX][Nu], favoured by primary substrates, inversion.
items.markingKey: SN1: two steps via a carbocation, rate = k[RX], favoured by tertiary substrates, racemisation; SN2: one concerted step, rate = k[RX][Nu], favoured by primary substrates, inversion. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a nucleophile and an electrophile.
items.answer: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor attracted to δ+ centres; an electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions.
items.markingKey: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor attracted to δ+ centres; an electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between an aprotic solvent and a protic solvent.
items.answer: A protic solvent has O–H or N–H bonds and solvates anions strongly (favours SN1); an aprotic solvent lacks them and leaves nucleophiles more reactive (favours SN2).
items.markingKey: A protic solvent has O–H or N–H bonds and solvates anions strongly (favours SN1); an aprotic solvent lacks them and leaves nucleophiles more reactive (favours SN2). items.stem: What is the rate equation for the reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with potassium cyanide in ethanol?

items.stem: Which of AlCl₃, CH₃NH₂, CH₃⁺ and NO₂⁺ can act as a nucleophile?

items.stem:

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Curly-arrow mechanisms are a realistic description of reactions."

items.stem: Explain the difference between a full-headed curly arrow and a fish-hook arrow.
items.answer: A full-headed arrow shows the movement of an electron pair (ionic mechanisms); a fish-hook arrow shows a single electron (radical mechanisms).

items.stem: A student claims: "A stronger nucleophile always increases the rate of substitution." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A stronger nucleophile increases the SN2 rate but has no effect on SN1, whose rate-determining step does not involve the nucleophile.

items.stem: Briefly explain why hydroxide ions are better nucleophiles than water molecules.
items.answer: OH⁻ carries a full negative charge, so its lone pairs are more available and it is more strongly attracted to the δ+ carbon.

items.stem: (R)-2-chlorobutane reacts with hydroxide ions by an SN2 mechanism. Predict the stereochemistry of the product and explain your answer.
